notes: characterization: Hostile portrait of Plancus's defection to Caesar on the eve of the war, attributing it to a treacherous nature; the author's moral verdict, not an event. (C. Velleius Paterculus 2.83.1, flagged)
interpretation: The author's claim that the outcome was settled before the fighting, with a partisan comparison of the two sides' morale, rowers and ships. (C. Velleius Paterculus 2.84.1, flagged)
interpretation: The author casts the battle as a contest between the world's safety (Caesar) and its ruin (Antony), a partisan moral verdict. (C. Velleius Paterculus 2.85.1, flagged)

interpretation: The author claims the outcome was settled when the fighting began, because one side had commander, rowers and soldiers and the other had soldiers alone. (C. Velleius Paterculus 2.85.3, flagged)

interpretation: The author infers from the clemency after Actium how moderate Caesar would have been in earlier victories, a partisan judgment in favour of Augustus and not an event. (C. Velleius Paterculus 2.86.2, flagged)

speech: Pollio's reported refusal to join Caesar at Actium, remaining aloof as the prize of the victor; it is rhetoric and the author's moral commentary on loyalty to Antony, not an event of the battle. (C. Velleius Paterculus 2.86.3, flagged)

interpretation: Dio's reading of the political situation before the war: after the loss of democracy, Antony and Caesar shared control on an equal footing while each tried to seize advantage over the other. This sets up the rivalry that leads to Actium. (Cassius Dio 50.1.1, flagged)
interpretation: Dio reads the open breach between the two rulers as the point at which the Roman people were actually reduced to slavery. (Cassius Dio 50.1.2, flagged)

motive: Dio gives Caesar's grievances against Antony over Cleopatra, her children, and Caesarion's place in Caesar's family, a reason for the rupture that preceded the war. (Cassius Dio 50.1.5, flagged)
motive: Dio gives Caesar's motive for taking the war to Greece, near Antony's bases, rather than fighting in Italy; this is a decision leading into the campaign. (Cassius Dio 50.11.4, flagged)

motive: Dio gives Caesar's reasons for gathering troops and influential men at Brundisium before crossing: to secure cooperation, prevent rebellion, and display the Roman support he held. (Cassius Dio 50.11.5, flagged)
anecdote: Dio reports only hearsay that Caesar hauled triremes into the gulf on oiled hides; he does not vouch for it. (Cassius Dio 50.12.5, flagged)
detail: Dio gives the overland transport of triremes to the gulf only as hearsay, and the next section says he doubts it; it is not asserted as fact. (Cassius Dio 50.12.5, flagged)

interpretation: Dio voices his own doubt about the tradition that Caesar's triremes were hauled over the fortifications into the gulf on oiled hides, while granting that the feat is said to have been done. (Cassius Dio 50.12.6, flagged)
motive: Dio gives Caesar's aim: to fight only the forces then present, before Antony's whole command assembled. (Cassius Dio 50.13.2, flagged)

speech: Dio's composed address for Caesar (Octavian): he explains why he did not treat Antony like Cleopatra. Cleopatra is an enemy through her foreign birth and conduct, while Antony, as a citizen, might still be brought to reason. This is rhetoric attributed to the speaker, not narrative fact. (Cassius Dio 50.26.3, flagged)

speech: Part of Caesar's pre-battle address, composed by Dio: rhetoric that casts Antony as bewitched by Cleopatra and fighting for her against Rome. It is not narrative fact. (Cassius Dio 50.26.5, flagged)

speech: Part of Dio's composed pre-battle address for Caesar, which abuses Antony as an Egyptian 'Serapion' and a mere gymnasiarch. This is rhetoric attributed to the speaker, not narrative fact. (Cassius Dio 50.27.1, flagged)

speech: Part of Caesar's pre-battle address composed by Dio: rhetoric reminding his soldiers of earlier campaigns against Sextus Pompey and Antony at Mutina, not narrative fact about Actium. (Cassius Dio 50.28.4, flagged)

detail: The preliminary war rites are performed through Caesar as fetialis. The passage states that the war was nominally against Cleopatra but really against Antony, which shows how Dio frames the opposition. (Cassius Dio 50.4.5, flagged)

motive: Dio explains why war was voted against Cleopatra and not against Antony: Antony would be an enemy anyway, and Rome wanted to blame him for voluntarily taking up war for the Egyptian woman against his own country. (Cassius Dio 50.6.1, flagged)

motive: Dio gives Caesar's purpose in sending the offer of battle terms: he did not expect acceptance but meant to raise his own men's courage and frighten the enemy. Antony is said to have mocked the proposal. (Cassius Dio 50.9.6, flagged)
interpretation: Dio singles out the date of the battle because from that day Caesar held sole power, so he treats Actium as the start of Caesar's sole rule. (Cassius Dio 51.1.1, flagged)
detail: Caesar's commemoration of the victory at Actium: dedications to Apollo of Actium from the captured ships, a larger temple, and the Actia games. (Cassius Dio 51.1.2, flagged)
interpretation: Dio explains why he gives the date of the battle: he reckons Caesar's sole rule, and so the years of his reign, from that day. (Cassius Dio 51.1.2, flagged)
interpretation: Dio reads the day of the battle as the start of Caesar's sole rule, so that the years of his reign are counted from it. (Cassius Dio 51.1.2, flagged)

characterization: Dio shows Caesar's reaction to Cleopatra's death after the Egyptian campaign: admiration and pity, and grief as if robbed of the glory of victory. This is not a claim about the Battle of Actium itself. (Cassius Dio 51.14.6, flagged)

motive: Dio explains Caesar's postponement of the Parthian appeals after the naval battle: the stated excuse was Egypt, but he really wanted the Parthians to exhaust each other. It is not a depiction of the battle itself. (Cassius Dio 51.18.2, flagged)

detail: Honours voted at Rome for Caesar's naval victory (Actium), including a triumph framed as over Cleopatra and two trophy arches; shows how the victory was received and framed at home. (Cassius Dio 51.19.1, flagged)

detail: Roman honours voted to Octavian after the naval victory: shrine of Julius adorned with captured ship beaks, a quadrennial festival, thanksgivings, and a formal reception on his return. (Cassius Dio 51.19.2, flagged)
